The fitness of an Alpha is a function of return, turnover and Sharpe. Good Alphas have high fitness. So please make sure the return and Sharpe are high and the turnover is low.
Return: Annual Return = annualized PnL / Size. It signifies the amount you made or lost during the period observed and is expressed in %
Turnover: It signifies how often one trades. Daily Turnover=Trading_volume / 2 * Size. Good Alphas have low turnover (Less than 40% is better).

3) These new Alpha values assigned to each stock are then converted to the amount of money allocated to a stock by scaling it to booksize.

This stock weight is thus nothing but the weight of the stock in the overall portfolio.

Let me give you a simple example, when Alpha = close.
Suppose you have a universe, with just 5 stocks (A, B, C, D,E) and on a particular date (20100104) they have the following close prices (in USD):

Instruments: A B C D E

close: 6 5 2 8 4

Now, you want to use the value of these close prices to calculate Alpha weights on the next trading day. You first start with the Alpha expression, which is Alpha = close. So you first make a vector of "close". i.e. (6, 5, 2, 8, 4). [Note: If your expression were Alpha = 1 / close, you'd have made a vector of "1 / close", i.e. (1/6, 1/5, 1/2, 1/8, 1/4) = (0.167, 0.2, 0.5, 0.125, 0.25). ]

Now you have the vector (6, 5, 2, 8, 4), this is not a vector of weights. A vector of weights needs to be normalized to 1. So we divide each element by the sum (= 25), so the sum of the elements equals 1.
So the new vector is: (6 / 25, 5 / 25, 2 / 25, 8 / 25, 4 / 25) = (0.24, 0.20, 0.08, 0.32, 0.16). The sum of this vector is 1. And this is our portfolio. We multiply this by the booksize (20 Million), and we get the amount of money we want to bet on each of the stocks.

This was the case when we have set Neutralization = "None". But this makes our strategy ride on market-risk. So, we select Neutralization = "Market". In this case again, we start out by creating a vector of "close" = (6, 5, 2, 8, 4).
Now we make it "mean-neutral", i.e subtract the mean (= 5) from each of the elements, making the sum of the vector = 0.
So the mean-neutral vector is: (1, 0, -3, 3, -1). You can see the sum of the elements is zero.

Now, in order to normalize, we need to ignore the sign and make the sum of elements = 1. So we calculate the sum of absolute values (= 1 + 0 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8). Now we divide each element by this sum, giving us (1 / 8, 0 / 8, -3 / 8, 3 / 8, -1 / 8) = (+0.125, 0, -0.375, +0.375, -0.125).
Now this is a normalized mean-neutral vector of weights. We multiply this by the booksize of 20 Million USD to get the amount we want to invest on each of the stocks, where a positive sign indicates taking long position and negative sign indicates taking short position. Also, since the positive values add up to +0.5 and the negative values add up to -0.5, we end up investing 10 Million in long and 10 Million in short positions, making the strategy dollar neutral as required.

answer:
[{"type": "TEXT", "value": "

Out of sample stats are available only after an Alpha has made a 'new high', in out sample.

In-Sample High: When you run a simulation, you see a cumulative PnL graph on the results page. This graph records your Alpha's performance in the In-Sample period which is from Apr 9, 2008 to Mar 8, 2013 (For 5 year simulation).

Now, the highest point in the PnL graph is your In-Sample 'high'. Let's say this In-Sample high occurs on Mar 1, 2013, at a PnL of 7.5 Million.

Out-Sample PnL: Now, suppose your Alpha gets selected for Out-Sample testing. The Out-Sample simulation begins just after the In-Sample ends, that is Mar 9, 2013, and goes on till today. Now, your PnL continues from where it left off, and Out-Sample PnL is also added to it. And we have an In-Sample + Out-Sample PnL performance of your Alpha.

Out-Sample High or New High in Out-Sample: Now, we look for a 'new high' in the Out-Sample period. That is, we look for a point in the Out-Sample portion of the performance(on or after Mar 9, 2013), where it crosses the In-Sample 'high' (7.5 Million in this example). Suppose it crosses this 7.5 Million mark on Apr 10, 2013. It means, that your Alpha has made its 'First New High' in Out-Sample on Apr 10, 2013. And now your OSSharpe ratio calculation can begin.

OS Sharpe Calculation: Sharpe30 would be the Sharpe ratio of your Alpha, for the first 30 days after Apr 10, 2013. That is, first 30 days after the 'First New High'.

OSSharpe would be the cumulative Sharpe ratio of your Alpha after the First New High, till today.

New High Occurring Late: In case, if your Alpha makes its First New High very late into the Out-Sample period. That is, suppose the Alpha in the above example, crosses the 7.5 Million mark on May 1, 2014 instead of Apr 10, 2013. Then there would be only around 50 trading days after May 1, 2014 till July 2014. So your Sharpe30 and Sharpe45 values could be calculated after the first new high, but Sharpe60, Sharpe85,etc could not be calculated, and you would have to wait for them even longer.

No New High: It could also happen that your Alpha does not make a new high at all. For example, if the above Alpha keeps going down in Out-Sample, and doesn't cross the In-Sample high mark of 7.5 Million till July 2014. It means that its First New High has not occurred till date. And its SharpeXX values and OSSharpe value would not get calculated.

Alphas are checked for New Highs every 2-3 weeks. If a new high has occurred then its OSSharpe values are calculated and displayed on the Out-Sample tab.

Status\u00a0represents your Alpha's current status whether it is IS-FAIL, OSTEST-PASS, OSTEST-PENDING, OSTEST-FAIL etc.\u00a0
If you simulate an Alpha, but it does not cross the Sharpe threshold then it is marked as IS-FAIL and is not considered for OS testing. If your Alpha does cross the threshold, then it is moved to OS tab and the status is changed to OSTEST-PENDING.

There are a variety of OS tests conducted on an Alpha, to check whether it is worthy or not. A few of these tests are:

SelfCorr: Checks the correlation of your Alpha with the rest of your OS Alphas. If an Alpha is uncorrelated, then it passes this test. Otherwise, only one out of a group of highly correlated Alphas passes the test.

ISSharpe\u00a0&\u00a0OSSharpe\u00a0Ladder tests: The ladder tests are there to determine whether the performance of an Alpha is "significant" or not. That is, whether it is possible to get the same performance from a random noise signal or not. If your Alpha's performance beats the performance of the purely random signal by some threshold, then your Alpha passes the ladder test, and we can be confident that it is indeed an Alpha and not just noise.

Kindly note few important points:

  • A status of OSTEST-DECM means that the alphas have failed out sample testing and will no longer be tested. Such alphas will not receive any scores.
  • A status of OSTEST-PENDING means that few tests have already been done on your alpha while few are still pending. On the other hand, OSTEST-FAIL implies that it has failed at least one of the tests in out sample testing. In both the cases, the alpha is eligible for scoring.
